coverage_notes: All six files were read in full with the Read tool (every line, in chunks): dllG2iXI2YQ (261 threads), dZTbJb5Nml8 (154), 4MxNB0BAjQE (250), wQMJdrJAyNI (53), YlthrT39ps8 (135), mwqWpDJzsog (97). Total 950 top-level comments plus replies. Counts are approximate hand tallies. A comment can carry several themes. Replies by other viewers that describe their own situation were counted as own-situation. Empty or near-empty gap lists: logins_passwords has no commenter mentioning passwords or logins at all; the two items listed are access-to-information barriers (bank statements, hospital not disclosing location) and are included only as the closest evidence. paying_for_tools has no commenter paying for software or an app; the items listed are paid services (lawyers) or paid care. tools_used_today is thin: commenters mention YouTube videos, internet searching, CCTV cameras, a calendar and two wellness apps. Non-aging care recipients (disabled child, autistic son, disabled adult daughter, mentally handicapped brother) and professional caregivers appear in the Mel Robbins and Julie videos and were not counted toward themes. Commenter names, one street address and one rambling post that appears to describe a nursing-home resident's own delusional experience were deliberately not quoted.

videos.title: The Do's and Don'ts of being a caregiver (yes, it's hard!)
videos.how_counted: Counted by hand while reading all 261 threads (about 25 to 30 of the replies also describe own situations). Approximate. T14 is mostly end-of-life/hospice caregiving and decisions about feeding, drinking and morphine; it overlaps with T8 and T12.
videos.audience_note: Hospice nurse channel, video about end of life care (do not force food or water, do not be hard on yourself). Commenters are mostly spouses and adult children who have just cared for, or are currently caring for, a dying person at home. Many arrive after the death and describe guilt and what-ifs. Many other comments are praise, prayers, questions to the nurse, religious posts, or hired caregivers and trainees. So the sample over-represents terminal illness, hospice and grief, not long-term chronic care.

videos.title: The Hidden Burnout Millions of Caregivers Are Facing | Mel Robbins #Shorts
videos.how_counted: Counted by hand over all 154 threads. Approximate. Nearly every own-situation comment carries T2, so T2 is close to the own-situation total. T14 is the number of commenters who care for a non-aging recipient (disabled child, autistic son, disabled spouse, brother) plus identity loss, post-caregiving depression and substance use.
videos.audience_note: Short video about caregiver burnout, with a general-audience celebrity host. Commenters are people in burnout: spouses, adult children (many daughters), parents of disabled children, hired carers and nurses. Many have no help and no siblings. Few describe logistics. It is almost entirely emotional load, isolation and the effect on the caregiver's own job, health, marriage and children.

videos.title: Important Dementia Behavior Tip #caregiving
videos.how_counted: Counted by hand over all 250 threads. Only about 55 describe a real caregiving situation; the rest are praise, jokes that redirecting is like parenting a toddler, and political jokes about public figures. Approximate.
videos.audience_note: Short dementia behavior tip (redirect, do not correct). Commenters mostly share tips or react that it is like raising a toddler, so the video draws a lot of advice and humor. The caregivers who do describe themselves ask for help with daily tasks (dressing, bathing, tooth brushing, mail, bills, repetitive behavior, aggression) and say redirection often fails or is exhausting. Dementia behavior dominates, almost no coordination or money content.

videos.title: Is Your Sibling Abusing Power of Attorney for an Elderly Parent? | Watch for These Warning Signs
videos.how_counted: Counted by hand over all 53 threads and their replies (including many creator replies, which were not counted). Approximate. T14 is the cluster of siblings or relatives cutting off a parent's visitors, information and communication (isolation of the parent, locked out of the parent's life).
videos.audience_note: Video aimed at people suspecting a sibling of misusing power of attorney. Commenters are mostly adult children in an active legal or financial dispute with a sibling, many of them excluded from the parent, locked out of information, or unable to afford a lawyer. They are not typical day-to-day caregivers: few describe hands-on care. The creator replies selling consultations.

videos.title: Why aging parents YELL at the caregiver who helps them MOST
videos.how_counted: Counted by hand over all 135 threads. Approximate. T14 is the cluster of being the scapegoat or target, parental favoritism (golden child), and unacknowledged caregiving.
videos.audience_note: Video explaining why aging parents lash out at the main caregiver. Commenters are mainly adult daughters and sons who were or are the main caregiver, many with a sibling who rarely visits but is praised, and many with a parent who is verbally abusive or has dementia. Strong resentment toward siblings and parents. Many comments are only thanks.

videos.title: One sibling ends up CAREGIVING. Why aging parents SPLIT families? How to AVOID it?
videos.how_counted: Counted by hand over all 97 threads. Approximate. T14 is the cluster about parental favoritism, golden child, sibling roles and who inherits the house.
videos.audience_note: Video about one sibling carrying all the caregiving. Commenters are siblings, mostly the one who did the work, describing uneven help, siblings who live far away, and later disputes over money and property. Some also show it working out (sisters sharing, a sibling paying). Coordination and fairness dominate, not the medical details.

new_themes.name: End-of-life and hospice home care decisions (eating, drinking, pain medicine)
new_themes.description: In the hospice video, most commenters are caring for or have just lost someone dying at home. They describe not knowing what to expect, guilt about decisions on feeding, hydration, morphine, hospital versus home, and uneven support from the hospice team.

example.quote: We demanded she eat, shower, move, get into her wheelchair, stay awake and up during the day (although she begged us to just sleep in bed all day).

new_themes.name: Being the target of anger, scapegoat, parental favoritism and unacknowledged caregiving
new_themes.description: Caregivers describe a parent who yells at or blames them while praising a sibling who rarely visits, and resentment that nobody acknowledges the work.

example.quote: I was never their favorite but I am still the only one helping them!

new_themes.name: Siblings or relatives controlling access to the parent (visits, information, records)
new_themes.description: Adult children locked out by a sibling holding power of attorney: not allowed to visit or call, not told where the parent is, not given bank statements or medical records, not told when the parent died.

example.quote: My sister has POA and she will no longer let me nor my daughter to visit nor call her.

new_themes.name: Estate, house and inheritance disputes tied to who did the caregiving
new_themes.description: Conflict over who lives in the parent's house, unequal pay for care, and fear of a fight over the estate after death; caregivers worry the work will be treated as a claim or as undue influence.

example.quote: My bro is expecting a 50/50 split and for the house to be sold.

new_themes.name: Life after caregiving: lost purpose, lasting health effects and role vacuum
new_themes.description: After the person dies, caregivers describe depression, loss of identity, health problems from the strain, and months or years to recover.

example.quote: And after it stops, after someone dies, you lose your purpose and get depressed and sometimes you never come back from it even years later.❤❤❤

new_themes.name: Untrained for physical care tasks (lifting, dressing, toileting, turning)
new_themes.description: Caregivers say nobody taught them hands-on tasks; they ask strangers online how to dress a spouse with dementia or move a bedbound person.

example.quote: As a caregiver we have no training on how to lift the patient, change soiled clothing and bed sheets, put them on a commode, lift them back into bed, administer medication and the list goes on and on.

new_themes.name: Respite exists but does not fit (location, all-or-nothing rules, not covered by insurance)
new_themes.description: Caregivers say respite care was offered but was far away, had to be taken all at once, or was not covered, so it went unused.

caveats: Comment samples are self-selected viewers of five very different videos and are not representative of all family caregivers. The Julie video skews to people at end of life and to commenters after a death; the POA video skews to disputes with a sibling; the sibling and yelling videos skew to resentment; the Mel Robbins video skews to burnout and includes carers of disabled children and hired carers; the dementia tip video is mostly jokes about toddlers. Many commenters are outside the United States (Australia, Ireland, India, Japan, Nigeria and others), some are children caring for a grandparent, and some are professional or trainee caregivers; US status is not stated for most and was not assumed. Counts are approximate hand tallies. Quote locators use COMMENT n for both top-level comments and their replies. Any quote that fails the machine match should be dropped. Sibling dispute and POA content describes accusations by one party only and none was verified. Creator replies in the POA file are marketing for paid consultations and were not counted as caregiver evidence.
